title: Matthew 27:45–56
context: From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covers the land. Jesus cries the forsaken cry of Psalm 22, yields up His spirit, the temple curtain tears, earth shakes, saints are raised, and a centurion confesses the Son of God while women watch from a distance.

verses.text: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour.
verses.arminianNotes:
Midday darkness—creation itself seems to mourn. The cross is not a private execution; the land is marked.

God gives signs that summon attention. Grace uses wonder to call; darkness still requires a response of faith in the Crucified.
verses.reformedNotes:
Darkness over the land: cosmic witness to the hour. Providence clothes Golgotha in night at noon.

Nature serves the Passion narrative. The Creator’s death-work is signaled in the creaturely sky.

verses.text: About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?” That is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The loud cry quotes Psalm 22: anguish, not playacting. The Holy One tastes forsakenness in our place.

Arminians stress sincere, costly atonement—Christ truly suffers for sinners whom grace invites to trust Him. The cry is not theater; it is the depth of redeeming love that enables faith rather than coerces it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Psalm 22 on the lips of the Son: forsakenness under judgment, yet still “My God.” The cry is covenantal anguish, not atheism.

Reformed heart of the cross: the cup is drained. Penal suffering and unbroken person of the Son hold together. He is forsaken in our stead according to the Father’s will, that the forsaken may be brought near.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse a mild cross. Arminians emphasize Christ’s loving self-giving that sincerely calls sinners to faith; Calvinists emphasize appointed substitution under the Father’s just will that will not fail to save His people.

verses.text: Some of them who stood there, when they heard it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They mishear Eli as Elijah. Even the cry of Scripture is garbled by unbelief.

Proximity to the cross does not equal understanding. Grace opens ears; without it, holy words become gossip.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mishearing at the cross: Elijah instead of Eli. Darkness of mind matches darkness of sky.

Human confusion cannot mute what Jesus actually prayed. The Word stands.

verses.text: Immediately one of them ran and took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him a drink.
verses.arminianNotes:
A sponge of sour wine on a reed—small mercy or further staging? Matthew records the act without flattery.

Mixed motives often surround holy suffering. Grace still calls bystanders from curiosity to faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sour wine offered: detail under providence, echoing Scripture’s thirst scenes.

Even a reed and sponge sit inside the fulfilled hour.

verses.text: The rest said, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to save him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wait—let us see: spectators want a show of rescue. Faith becomes watching for spectacle.

Delaying for signs can be unbelief dressed as patience. Grace points to the Christ already saving by staying.
verses.reformedNotes:
The crowd treats watching for Elijah as entertainment. They miss the salvation happening in the cry itself.

There will be no Elijah show. Deliverance will be resurrection, not their demanded stunt.

verses.text: Jesus cried again with a loud voice, and yielded up his spirit.
verses.arminianNotes:
Loud voice, then yielded spirit—death is concrete, and also given. He lays down life; it is not merely ripped away.

Jesus dies willingly for sinners. Grace invites trust in the One who yielded Himself, not in our climbing down from guilt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Yielded up His spirit: authority in dying. The Son’s life is not stolen at random.

Obedient death under the Father. The Spirit is yielded when the work of that hour is complete.

verses.text: Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. The earth quaked and the rocks were split.
verses.arminianNotes:
Curtain torn from top to bottom—access language in fabric. Earth shakes; rocks split. God interprets the death with holy violence against barriers.

The way to God is opened in Christ for all who come. Grace invites bold approach; do not sew the curtain back with self-made religion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Torn top to bottom: God acts from above. Earthquake signs the verdict of heaven on the cross.

Atonement opens the holy place. The barrier falls by God’s hand, not human ladders.

verses.text: The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised;
verses.arminianNotes:
Tombs open; sleeping saints are raised—firstfruits atmosphere around the Crucified. The reign of death begins to crack.

The cross unleashes life. Grace that raises is offered in the gospel to those who believe.
verses.reformedNotes:
Opened tombs: the death of Jesus shakes Sheol’s gates. Matthew ties resurrection power to this death.

The Crucified is already Lord over death’s domain. Providence previews Easter in the quake.

verses.text: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered into the holy city and appeared to many.
verses.arminianNotes:
Matthew times their appearance after His resurrection—Christ first. Witnesses in the holy city multiply testimony.

God gives evidence that calls for faith. Appearances invite responsible trust, not coerce robots.
verses.reformedNotes:
After His resurrection they appear: order preserved—Christ the firstfruits logic.

Jesus’ rising governs theirs. The holy city receives signs that the age to come has broken in.

verses.text: Now the centurion and those who were with him watching Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were done, were terrified, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God!”
verses.arminianNotes:
A Gentile watch confesses: Truly this was the Son of God. The title mocked earlier is spoken in awe.

Grace reaches unexpected mouths. The confession is a response to light given; hearers may likewise confess.
verses.reformedNotes:
Centurion’s confession from the guard post. Providence draws praise from Rome’s own ranks.

The Son is acknowledged even at the cross. God opens eyes according to mercy; the confession stands as true.
verses.keyContrast: Both treasure the confession. Arminians typically underline enabled, responsible response to revealed awe; Reformed commentators stress God’s merciful opening of Gentile lips amid the appointed Passion.

verses.text: Many women were there watching from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Women watch from a distance—faithful presence when many disciples fled. Ministry from Galilee continues at the cross.

Grace sustains quiet fidelity. Distance may be forced by danger; love still looks on.
verses.reformedNotes:
Women as witnesses: Matthew prepares Easter testimony. Providence keeps observers at the death.

God often preserves the story through overlooked servants. Their watching is part of the plan of witness.

verses.text: Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
verses.arminianNotes:
Named women: Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, Zebedee’s wife. Love with names attached.

For the reader: discipleship is personal. Grace calls particular people to particular courage at the cross.
verses.reformedNotes:
Names recorded under the cross. Scripture remembers who stayed near.

God writes witnesses into the Passion so the church may know this death was public, attested, and unto hope.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On the forsaken cry, the yielded spirit, and the opened way through Christ’s death, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Now they are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ. Him God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood.… Now hath Christ taken away the curse of the law, being made a curse for us… blotting out the handwriting that was against us… nailing it to his cross.

I know, the saints who will be placed before the tribunal of the Divine Justice, have had Faith, and through Faith have performed good Works. But… they appear and stand before God with this confidence… that God has set forth his Son Jesus Christ as a propitiation through Faith in his blood… I do not read, that Christ is constituted a propitiation through Works… that we may also be justified by Works.
arminian.source: Works, Vol. 1 (on justification / faith and works)

reformed.quote: Nor is it by hypocrisy, or by assuming a character, that he complains of having been forsaken by the Father.… the inward sadness of his soul was so powerful and violent, that it forced him to break out into a cry.… having undertaken to be our surety, he resolved actually to undergo in our room the judgment of God.… Though the perception of the flesh would have led him to dread destruction, still in his heart faith remained firm… before stating the temptation, he begins by saying that he betakes himself to God as his God.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 27:46)

reformed.quote: What do you understand by the word “suffered”? That during his whole life on earth, but especially at the end, Christ sustained in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. This he did in order that, by his suffering as the only atoning sacrifice, he might deliver us, body and soul, from eternal condemnation, and gain for us God’s grace, righteousness, and eternal life.
